title: Rights groups condemn 'racist murder' of Manipuri singer in Delhi, demand racial-motive probe
excerpt: Civil society and human rights organisations say the mob killing of musician Chongtham Vikram Singh must be examined in the wider context of racial violence against people from Northeast India.
body:
• A coalition of civil society and human rights organisations has condemned the killing of Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh, 54, in Delhi as a "racist murder" and demanded a thorough probe into a possible racial motive.
  • Vikram was beaten by a mob of eight men in South Delhi's Ashram area around 11:30 pm on September 6 after objecting to loud noise outside his home; he died at Holy Family Hospital at 6 am the next day.
  • The groups — including the Manipur Students' Association Delhi and Human Rights Alert — met on September 8 and cited unimplemented 2014 Bezbaruah Committee recommendations and the absence of a comprehensive anti-racial-discrimination law.
  • Union Minister Kiren Rijiju said all eight accused have been arrested and promised a watertight chargesheet; hundreds held a candlelight vigil for Vikram in Imphal on September 9.

What: Rights organisations condemn the mob killing of Manipuri singer Chongtham Vikram Singh in Delhi as a "racist murder." When: Attacked late on September 6; joint statement issued September 8. Where: Ashram area, South Delhi. Why it matters: The case has become a flashpoint for long-standing concerns about racial violence against people from Northeast India.

A group of civil society and human rights organisations has condemned the death of Manipuri music teacher and singer Chongtham Vikram Singh, who was allegedly killed by a mob in Delhi on Sunday night, calling it a "racist murder" and demanding a thorough investigation into the possible racial motive behind the attack.

The joint statement followed a September 8 meeting at the Centre for Equity Studies in New Delhi of six organisations, including the Manipur Students' Association Delhi, People's Progressive Alliance Manipur, Karwan-e-Mohabbat and Human Rights Alert.

What happened

According to his wife, Joshna Chongtham, the tragedy unfolded around 11:30 pm on September 6, when the 54-year-old musician went downstairs from his residence in South Delhi's Ashram area to object to loud noise from delivery boys and dhaba staff. What began as a request to lower the volume escalated: Singh was chased to his doorstep and beaten with fists and heavy blows by eight men, who fled when family members opened the door.

Suffering from severe breathlessness and a rapid drop in blood pressure, Singh was rushed by his son to the Holy Family Hospital emergency room, where he succumbed to his injuries at 6:00 am on Monday, September 7.

"I have lost my husband, and my son lost his father. My husband was a peace-loving musician who lived a peaceful life... We hope such an incident never happens to another family, and we hope justice will be done," Joshna Chongtham said.

The accused have been identified as workers at dhabas and food stalls in the area: seven adults arrested and one juvenile apprehended. FIR 0296 at Sunlight Colony police station invokes Sections 103(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — Section 103(2) covers mob murder on grounds including race.

The rights groups' case

The organisations said Vikram's killing should not be treated as an isolated criminal incident but examined in the wider context of racial prejudice and violence faced by people from Northeast India. They described the police investigation so far as inadequate to address what they called a broader pattern of racist crimes against the community.

The statement pointed to the MP Bezbaruah Committee, set up by the Home Ministry, whose 2014 recommendations — including a proposal to specifically criminalise racist acts — remain largely unimplemented. It cited the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination's August 2026 call for comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation, and noted that Article 15 of the Constitution does not expressly list colour, descent or ethnic origin.

"Justice for Chongtham Vikram is not merely a demand for accountability for one murder. It is a demand for dignity, equality, security, and the fundamental right to live free from racial violence for all people from Northeast India."

— Joint statement of civil society and human rights organisations

The groups demanded an impartial, transparent investigation — including an evidence-based examination of any racial motive — plus support, protection and compensation for Vikram's family. The meeting ended with a two-minute silence in his memory.

Political response and protests

Union Minister Kiren Rijiju said on Tuesday that all eight accused had been arrested and promised a watertight chargesheet, adding that Singh's mortal remains would be taken to Manipur on Wednesday. Police have said no racial motive has been established so far and that the investigation continues.

The killing has triggered protests in Delhi and outrage across the Northeast. Hundreds of people gathered at Kangla Western Gate in Imphal on Tuesday for a candlelight vigil paying tribute to the musician, while opposition leaders — including a Congress MP — targeted the Modi government over the safety of Northeastern citizens in the capital.

Diaspora angle

For the Northeastern diaspora abroad, the case is being watched as a measure of how India confronts racial violence at home — a concern that shapes how safe the community feels both in Indian cities and in conversations with the wider world.

What comes next

The immediate test is the chargesheet and whether investigators examine the racial dimension the rights groups insist cannot be ignored. Beyond the courtroom, the case has revived a decade-old demand — comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation — that will show whether this killing becomes a turning point or another entry in a familiar pattern.
